title: Answering for Your Level
summary: The same competency question needs a bigger 'we' at every level up. Learn how scope, ownership, and the size of the outcome you claim should shift between IC, senior, and staff+/manager answers to the same behavioral question.

slides.markdown:
"Tell me about a conflict" gets asked identically at every level, but the bar for a strong answer moves sharply as the target level goes up. A junior candidate telling an IC-scope conflict story at a staff loop isn't wrong — it's just answering the wrong-sized question.

This topic is about scope calibration: the same archetype (from two topics ago) and the same company framework (from the last topic) both need to be delivered at the right altitude. Interviewers scoring a senior or staff loop are explicitly checking whether you operate at that scope, not just whether the underlying skill exists.

slides.sectionTitle: An IC-level vs. a staff-level answer to the same question
slides.subTitle: Compare
slides.markdown:
Question: "tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement."

| | IC-level answer | Staff-level answer |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Disagreement with one teammate over a code review comment | Disagreement between two teams over which service owns a shared data model |
| Action | Explained reasoning, teammate agreed | Ran a working session with both teams' leads, proposed a shared ownership boundary, got sign-off from both EMs |
| Outcome | PR merged, relationship intact | Boundary adopted org-wide, prevented three future similar disputes |
| "I" vs. "we" | "I explained why my approach was safer" | "I decided we needed a written ownership doc, and drove both teams to sign off on it" |

Both are legitimate, honest answers — they're just calibrated to different scope. Neither is a lie; the mismatch happens when a candidate targeting staff tells the left column's story.

Interviewers listen for a specific scope signal early in your answer, often in the first sentence, and calibrate their follow-ups to it:

- **Individual task scope:** "I fixed a bug that was causing..." — appropriate for entry-level, red flag as your only register at senior+.
- **Team scope:** "our team decided to..." or "I led my team to..." — the expected default for mid-level/senior.
- **Cross-org scope:** "I got three teams aligned on..." or "this affected how the whole org handles..." — the expected register for staff+ and management-track roles.

A candidate should be able to state, in one sentence, the scope of the story they're about to tell, and that scope should roughly match the level they're interviewing for across most of their answers — one story below level is fine; several stories consistently below level reads as a genuine level mismatch.

slides.sectionTitle: Talking about impact with real metrics at increasing seniority
slides.markdown:
The kind of metric that reads as impressive also shifts with level. A junior candidate citing "reduced query time by 40%" on their own service is a solid, appropriately-scoped number. A staff candidate citing the same kind of single-service metric, with nothing broader attached, under-signals — the expected metric at that level is closer to "the pattern we established got adopted by four other teams and reduced incident rate 25% org-wide."

This doesn't mean staff candidates need bigger absolute numbers — it means the metric needs to reflect a bigger *radius of effect*: did the outcome change how one function worked, or how a team works, or how the org works. Practice restating your existing metrics in terms of radius, not just magnitude, before a senior-level loop.

slides.sectionTitle: When "I" should become "I decided, and here's how the team executed"
slides.markdown:
A subtle language shift matters more than candidates expect. "I built X" at senior+ level, told about work that clearly involved a team, can read as either taking undue credit or a sign you don't delegate — both bad signals for a role that's supposed to scale beyond individual output.

The stronger construction separates decision from execution: "I decided we should restructure the pipeline this way, and here's how I got the team aligned and what they built." This gives credit accurately (the team executed) while still being honest about your specific contribution (you made the call, or drove the alignment). It's not modesty for its own sake — it's precision about what you actually did versus what the team did, which is exactly what a staff-level interviewer is trying to isolate.

slides.sectionTitle: Preparing a story that demonstrates the next level up
slides.markdown:
A useful, concrete prep habit: for every level you're interviewing at, keep at least one story in your bank that's honestly scoped **one level above** your current target — not exaggerated, just a real instance where you operated with bigger scope than your day-to-day title implies.

Many engineers have at least one such story even before an official promotion: covering for an absent lead during a launch, driving a cross-team decision because no one else stepped up, mentoring someone into a role you used to hold. Having this ready lets you answer a loop's occasional "show me you're ready for the next level" probe directly, instead of only being able to demonstrate your current, already-proven scope.

slides.sectionTitle: A staff candidate's story that stays at IC scope
slides.markdown:
The most common way strong ICs stall at a staff loop: every story is real, well-told, and technically excellent, but every single one is scoped to "I personally solved a hard problem" with no story about aligning people, setting direction for others, or absorbing ambiguity on behalf of a team.

This is rarely dishonest — it's usually that the candidate's actual day-to-day work is still mostly IC-scoped, and their story bank accurately reflects that. The fix isn't fabricating scope you don't have; it's being honest with yourself before the loop about whether your current stories genuinely support the level you're targeting, and either finding the real cross-team or ambiguity-absorbing stories you do have, or recalibrating which level to target.

slides.sectionTitle: Calibration checklist before a senior+ loop
slides.markdown:
Run through your top 4-5 stories and check each one against:

- Does the first sentence make the scope (individual/team/cross-org) clear without me having to explain it later?
- Is the metric framed by radius of effect, not just magnitude?
- Do I say "I decided" for the parts I actually decided, and credit the team for what they executed?
- Do I have at least one story that's honestly one level above my current scope?

If most of your stories fail two or more of these, that's a signal to either recalibrate which level you're targeting or to spend prep time finding better-scoped material rather than over-polishing the delivery of under-scoped stories.

slides.sectionTitle: Calibration is a lens on every archetype, not a separate skill
slides.markdown:
Everything in this topic layers on top of what's already in your bank — it's not a new set of stories to build, it's a scope check applied to the ones you already have. A conflict story, an ambiguity story, an influence story: each can be told at IC scope or staff scope with the same underlying honesty, just a different radius.

The next topics turn to a different lens on the same material: the specific answer patterns — badmouthing, over-claiming credit, no real reflection — that actively damage a story regardless of how well-scoped it otherwise is.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in a debrief
slides.markdown:
Behind the scenes, a hiring committee reviewing a staff-loop packet is often explicitly asking "did this candidate demonstrate staff-level scope, or IC-level scope told well." A debrief note like "strong stories but consistently IC-scoped" is a common, specific reason for a level-down offer or a no-hire, even when every individual answer was technically excellent.

Knowing this in advance is exactly why scope calibration deserves deliberate prep time rather than being left to how the conversation naturally unfolds — it's one of the few things about a behavioral round you can meaningfully control ahead of time.
